note_claims.claim: The patient has had a cough and coryza for 4 days.
The patient has had increased work of breathing since yesterday.
The patient has had coryza and cough for 4 weeks.
The patient's breathing has been fast since yesterday.
The patient's temperature has been up to 37.9 °C.
The patient has been feeding about half his usual amount since yesterday.
The patient has had four wet nappies in 24 hours.
The patient has no history of apnoea (older sister had an apnoea with bronchiolitis two years ago).
The patient has no cyanosis.
The patient has had a small posset after coughing.
The patient was born at 39 weeks with no neonatal problems.
The patient has no cardiac or respiratory history.
The patient's immunisations are up to date.
The patient has taken Calpol once yesterday.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The patient's temperature is 37.8 °C.
The patient's respiratory rate (RR) is 54 times a minute.
The patient's heart rate (HR) is 150.
The patient's oxygen level (SpO2) is 95 percent in air.
The patient exhibits intercostal and subcostal recession (pulling in between ribs and under them) when breathing.
The patient's capillary refill time (CRT) is under two seconds.
The patient is alert and looking around.
The patient's weight is 8.2 kg (50th centile).
The patient has bilateral fine crackles and wheeze.
The impression is Bronchiolitis with increased work of breathing (intercostal recession) and feeds about 50% of usual.
The plan is a clinical review tomorrow morning.
The plan is to give small, frequent feeds and saline nose drops before feeds in the meantime.
The patient is advised that the illness may worsen over days 3–5.
Safety-netting is to call the practice back if unable to attend within the hour, so an ambulance can be arranged.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician greeted the patient and their parents.
The patient has had a runny nose and a cough for four days.
Since yesterday, the patient's breathing has been really fast.
The patient is seven months old.
The patient had a temperature of 37.9 this morning.
The patient was initially reported as taking most of his bottles.
The patient is only managing about half of each bottle since yesterday.
The father did the night feeds.
The patient keeps pulling off to breathe.
The patient has had four wet nappies in the last 24 hours.
The patient usually has six or seven wet nappies.
The patient's older sister had an apnoea with bronchiolitis two years ago.
The sister stopped breathing in the night and they had to call an ambulance.
The patient has no history of apnoea.
The patient has no cyanosis.
The patient brought up a bit of milk after coughing.
The patient was born at 39 weeks with no problems.
The patient has no cardiac or respiratory history.
The patient's immunisations are up to date.
The patient has taken Calpol once yesterday.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The father smokes, but only outside, never in the house.
The patient's temperature is 37.8 °C.
The patient's respiratory rate is about 54 times a minute.
The patient's heart rate is 150.
The patient's oxygen level is 95 percent.
The patient is pulling in between his ribs and under them when he breathes (working hard).
The patient's capillary refill is under two seconds.
The patient is alert and looking around.
The clinician can hear crackles and some wheeze on both sides of the chest.
The findings (crackles and wheeze) fit with bronchiolitis, a common virus in babies.
The clinician plans to see the patient at the hospital today.
The clinician will ring the paediatric team.
The paediatric team can keep an eye on his breathing, help with feeds, and give him oxygen or other treatment if needed.
The clinician advises giving smaller feeds more often until the patient gets to the hospital.
The clinician advises saline drops in the nose before feeds to help clear it.
Bronchiolitis often gets worse over the first three to five days before it gets better.
If the patient has any pauses in his breathing, goes blue, or is really struggling to breathe, they should call 999.
The patient should go straight to the hospital.
If the patient cannot get there within the hour, they should ring back and an ambulance will be arranged.
